News.title: Trump loses it with reporter over Iran question: 'You wouldn't be here without me!'
News.content:
Trump loses it with reporter over Iran question: 'You wouldn't be here without me!'

The 47th President of the United States has lashed out at a reporter who asked about skyrocketing fuel prices.

View Image Donald Trump (Image: Getty Images)

Donald Trump has lashed out at a reporter who asked how he planned to combat skyrocketing fuel prices for the everyday American, with the US President replying with a long-winded rant about Iran and nuclear missiles. The cost of fuel in America, meanwhile, sits at USD$4 per gallon, which is about £3; the highest price since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Trump was taking questions from reporters at the White House on Tuesday after signing an executive order cracking down on mail-in voting, and when he was confronted with the question on the latest eye-watering cost of fuel.

Article continues below

But, instead of answering the cost-of-living question, Trump argued that even though Americans are paying more for fuel, they feel “safer” thanks to his strikes against Iran, which have, in turn, caused fuel prices to skyrocket. The 47th US President added that the conflict with Iran will wrap up in a matter of weeks. Here is the US President's full response to a reporter asking what he was doing to combat rising gas prices: "All I have to do is leave Iran, and we’ll be doing that very soon. And [fuel prices will] come tumbling down. And stock prices were up today almost to a record because they know two things: Number one, we have a safe country. We had to take a little detour because we had a madman named [Iran's former Supreme Leader Ali] Khamenei, who, sadly, is no longer with us. "And we had regime change already. We’ve knocked out one regime, then we knocked out the second regime. Now we have a group of people that’s very different. They’re much more reasonable, I think much more, much less radicalised. We’re dealing with people that are much more rational. And it’s very, it’s amazing what we’ve done. We had to make a little detour. "So when the stock market broke all records just a few weeks ago, when it hit 50,000 on the Dow, 7,000 and the S&P, I said to the American people, it’s time that we have to make a little detour, because we have a madman that wants a nuclear weapon, and if we did not knock him out B-52 bomber, we would have a nuclear weapon right now. "It would have been used before this, before today. And you may not be standing there asking that question, okay?" The US President did not divulge what measures would be taken, if any, to assist the everyday American to pay at the bowser. Trump's lack of response comes as the UK government has hinted at fresh measures to prevent a fuel shortage and ensure emergency vehicles have priority. Downing Street has insisted petrol stations remain well-stocked after recent images show numerous garages "running out" of supply as people begin stockpiling over fears of increased prices. The disruption has been caused by Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz - a critical route through which around a fifth of the world's oil passes. However, as Keir Starmer met with industry leaders to assess the situation, officials confirmed the Government is preparing for "all eventualities" should the war escalate further. As part of this, certain sectors and vehicles will receive priority over others to ensure they are able to complete daily, essential jobs. Supplies could also be restricted to certain times of day, while oil companies may be directed to prioritise deliveries to critical sectors. For example, emergency vehicles like ambulances and police cars will receive priority over those who are able to complete tasks from home. In addition, speed limits could be reduced to cut overall fuel consumption - a measure previously recommended by the International Energy Agency. This would mean less fuel is burned, resulting in less of a need for cars to refuel. Experts have suggested that relatively simple steps could help ease pressure on supplies if needed. These include encouraging people to work from home, increasing public transport use and reducing non-essential travel, as well as scaling back some domestic flights.

News.title: UK lagging dangerously behind on tackling extremism, chilling study by MPs finds
News.content:
UK lagging dangerously behind on tackling extremism, chilling study by MPs finds

The Home Affairs Committee found the flagship counter-terrorism Prevent programme is not equipped to deal with alarming online groups such as 'com networks' spreading dangerous hate online

View 2 Images Axel Rudakubana was referred to the flagship Prevent programme three times before the Southport attack in 2024 (Image: PA)

The UK is lagging dangerously behind in dealing with new forms of extremism, a probe by MPs has found.

‌



Ministers have been warned that flagship counter-terror programme Prevent is outdated and inadequately equipped to deal with emerging challenges. A damning report today warns that online networks targeting children - and sick influencers saying dangerous things to make money - are not being tackled fast enough.

‌



MPs said authorities have too little understanding how online misogyny, antisemitism, conspiracy theories and violence are radicalising young and vulnerable people. The report said 'com networks', groups known to encourage sexual extortion, violent crime and neo-Nazism, are a "serious and escalating threat".

‌



And it warned that social media, gaming platforms, online forums and influencers are spreading extremist material faster than it can be taken down.

The findings, by the cross-party Home Affairs Committee, came after it emerged Southport killer Axel Rudakubana had been referred to Prevent three times - but each time his case was closed because he was not deemed a terrorism risk.

Tory turncoat who sued old party for changing office locks suffers disaster in court READ MORE :

View 2 Images Bebe King, Elsie Dot Stancombe, and Alice Da Silva Aguiar died in the Southport attack (Image: PA)

‌



He went on to kill three girls and injure 10 others in a horrifying attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance party in 2024. MPs said the programme has become over-saturated with referrals, with many of those flagged having no clear ideology but displaying a fascination with violence. Neuro divergent people are over-represented in referrals, the report states.

Dame Karen Bradley, who chairs the committee, said: "Many of the core functions designed to divert children and young people at risk of being radicalised were established in a different age.

"Prevent has the clear and explicit function of stopping people becoming radicalised into terrorism, but more and more it is having to support those with no ideological motivation, who may have complex needs and operate in digital spaces that are poorly understood.

‌



“There needs to be a comprehensive structure in place at a local level, but implemented nationwide, that triages referrals to where they can receive the right support."

During the inquiry, Imran Ahmed, Chief Executive at the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, said social media firms are turning a blind eye to the role they play.

He told MPs: "When you go home tonight, I want you to record a video of yourself and put five seconds of Taylor Swift’s latest song in the background and try uploading it to YouTube and see how fast their algorithms can identify her song and [shut down your video].

Article continues below

"They (tech companies) know exactly how to do this. They have been doing it for a decade when it comes to copyrighted material, and yet when it comes to content that make our kids cut themselves or might lead to a terrorist attack, they somehow cannot do it."

The report said teaching young people to analyse online material critically and identify AI deepfakes is a key step.

News.title: Parents told impact of kids' behaviour on lessons - as private schools perform better
News.content:
Parents told impact of kids' behaviour on lessons - as private schools perform better

Two-thirds of state-school teachers (66%) in England say pupil behaviour has a negative impact on learning in lessons either regularly or all the time, a poll shows

View 2 Images More than a quarter (26%) of state-school teachers said behaviour negatively impacts lessons 'all the time' (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Two-thirds of state-school teachers (66%) in England say pupil behaviour has a negative impact on learning in lessons either regularly or all the time, a poll shows.

‌



Just 8% said it “rarely” or “never” has an impact on classrooms - compared to almost a third of teachers (31%) in private schools, according to a major survey by the National Education Union.

‌



Some 40% of teachers in state schools said behaviour impacts lessons “often or regularly”, while more than a quarter (26%) said it happens “all the time”. It is similar to last year’s figures, when 67% said behaviour negatively impacted lessons regularly or all the time, but much higher than the 48% in 2022 and 46% in 2020.

‌



Across state schools, primary settings or specialist provision suffered more from disruption. Some 70% of teachers in primary schools said behaviour was having an impact, as did 69% in special schools or pupil referral units.

Students' racist and misogynistic behaviour exposed as extreme online content fears grow READ MORE :

View 2 Images Daniel Kebede, the NEU’s general secretary, said: “Many teachers are worried about the impact of challenging behaviour on learning in their lessons." (Image: PA)

Teachers working in high deprivation settings were also more likely to say that student behaviour had a negative impact on learning in their lessons, the study found.

‌



Teachers referenced a lack of resources and staffing, unmet needs of students with regard to SEND and the impact of social media use among the causes of challenging behaviour. One teacher told the survey: “Due to unmet SEND needs and insufficient specialist provision, staff are increasingly required to manage complex behaviours without adequate support or intervention from senior leadership.”

Another said: “Increasing exposure to concerning attitudes and beliefs on the internet: misogyny is clearly having a huge effect, especially as a female teacher when dealing with the behaviour of male students.”

A separate NEU survey yesterday(TUE) found extreme online content and personalities are triggering racist, misogynistic and hateful behaviours among pupils

‌



Teachers also cited a rigid curriculum, that is often inappropriate for some students, as a cause of disruption in classrooms. One teacher told the survey the curriculum is “overloaded”, with “too much expected of the children in a short space of time”.

Overall, more teachers feel supported by their school’s behaviour policy (43%) - though more than a third still feel unsupported (34%).

The NEU said the different outcomes between state and private schools showed “the roles that resourcing, class size and pupil to adult ratios play in behaviour”. For state schools, the average class size is 26.4 pupils for primary schools and 22.5 for secondary. The typical class size at a private school is between 10 and 15 pupils, according to School Scout.

Article continues below

Daniel Kebede, the NEU’s general secretary, said: “Many teachers are worried about the impact of challenging behaviour on learning in their lessons. Schools need behaviour management policies that staff can rely on in practice. In too many settings, this confidence is lacking.”

::: The NEU conducted an online survey of 10,715 teacher members and 3,274 support staff members between February 5 and 16.

News.title: Watchdog issues Stephen Lawrence warning over police racism progress - 'trust is broken'
News.content:
Watchdog issues Stephen Lawrence warning over police racism progress - 'trust is broken'

The watchdog overseeing the Police Race Action Plan found progress is 'far too dependent on individual goodwill rather than wholesale commitment from police leadership'

View 2 Images Stats out in 2024 show Black men were 2.4 times as likely to be arrested as white men (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Police have produced “limited, inconsistent and fragile progress” in tackling racism - five years on from a plan launched in the wake of George Floyd’s murder in 2020, a grim report warns today(WED).

‌



The watchdog overseeing the Police Race Action Plan (PRAP) has found progress is “far too dependent on individual goodwill rather than wholesale commitment from police leadership”.

‌



In its report, the Independent Scrutiny and Oversight Board (ISOB) said just six of the 44 forces covered by the PRAP have publicly acknowledged institutional racism.

‌



Abimbola Johnson, the ISOB’s chairwoman, warned the slow progress of reforms “mirrors the pattern” of change in the wake of the Macpherson inquiry into Stephen Lawrence’s murder. The report into the racist murder of the 18-year-old in 1993 found the Metropolitan Police had been incompetent and was institutionally racist.

Stats out in 2024 show Black men were 2.4 times as likely to be arrested as white men and Black people were 3.7 times more likely to be stopped and searched compared to white people.

View 2 Images Abimbola Johnson, the watchdog chair, said: 'Progress has been slow, uneven and too dependent on individual effort rather than institutional change'

‌



Ms Johnson said: “Five years ago, policing committed to improving outcomes for Black communities. That commitment has not been met. Progress has been slow, uneven and too dependent on individual effort rather than institutional change.

“Black communities now deserve structural accountability. Government and policing must decide whether to deliver it or allow reform to stall again.”

Sarah Crew, chief constable at Avon and Somerset Police, told ISOB's report that "acknowledging institutional racism is only the starting point".

‌



She continued: "Black communities have heard the same discussions since the murder of Stephen Lawrence a quarter of a century ago. Words alone are not enough. Trust has been broken. We must show, not just say, that this time is different."

Chief Constable Gavin Stephens, chair of the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said: “There is no doubt that policing has made huge strides in certain areas under the Police Race Action Plan (PRAP) since it launched, thanks to the commitment of thousands of people both inside and outside policing.” But he admitted he shared the ISOB’s conclusion that “there is still far more work to be done”.

He continued: “Progress in this area has been inconsistent, too often dependent on committed individuals and not driven by the kind of systemic and deep rooted cultural change I and many others envisaged at the outset of this plan.

‌



“PRAP will continue in a new guise with a strong operational focus on anti-racism and it is vital that leaders across policing continue to recognise its importance and remain committed to deliver a service that earns the trust and confidence of all our officers, staff and communities we serve.”

The PRAP sets out the ambition of police chiefs in England and Wales to address race disparities affecting Black people working within or interacting with policing. The ISOB report calls on the Home Office to establish and fund independent scrutiny, mandate national data standards and embed race equity within inspection and performance frameworks.

The publication of the ISOB report comes as the Police Race Action Plan comes to an end as a standalone programme.

Article continues below

The board warns that progress now depends on embedding accountability within core systems, including the inclusion of race metrics in the His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services inspection framework and direct Home Office oversight.

News.title: Fitness influencer's poignant final selfie hours before her death in motorbike crash
News.content:
Fitness influencer's poignant final selfie hours before her death in motorbike crash

Larissa da Silva Machado, dressed in a black dress during an evening with friends, smiles for the camera — oblivious the snap would be her last selfie

View 3 Images Larissa da Silva Machado is seen in the last selfie she posted online (Image: JamPress)

Larissa da Silva Machado smiles for a selfie on a night out.

‌



But just hours later, she had died — having been involved in a horrific motorbike crash. Tributes have now poured in for Larissa, 30, who had built a following of around 20,000 on Instagram, where she shared fitness tips and healthy lifestyle content.

‌



The young woman, who was from Brazil, is believed to have lost control of her Honda CG 160 Titan on the lower ramp of a viaduct before smashing into a retaining wall on Friday. She was thrown several metres from the bike and suffered fatal head injuries.

‌



However, on Thursday night, Larissa had enjoyed an evening with friends, stepping away from the gang to take a smiling selfie in the venue.

Friends, thought to be the same pals, were following Larissa in a car behind her when the smash unfolded in Manaus, Brazil. They witnessed the crash, which saw the social media star flung a significant distance from the motorbike.

Hit-and-run driver carried on delivering Chinese takeaway after leaving dad to die READ MORE :

3 View 3 Images The 30-year-old woman was known for her fitness tips and advice (Image: JamPress) 3 View 3 Images Larissa shared several pictures of her wearing a motorbiking helmet, though this picture was not taken on Friday (Image: JamPress)

‌



One of Larissa's friends rang the woman's mum in the minutes after the collision — who rushed to the scene in shock. The distraught mother had to be restrained by police as she ran towards her daughter's body. She cried out: "Let me see my daughter, let me go, I want to see my daughter."

Emergency crews rushed to the scene, but Larissa could not be saved. Her motorbike was completely destroyed by the force of the impact. Authorities later confirmed she died from a traumatic brain injury.

Police have since cordoned off the area and launched an investigation into the fatal crash. Officers are analysing CCTV footage to piece together exactly what happened in the moments leading up to the tragedy.

‌



At the time of her death, Larissa had built a following of around 20,000 on Instagram, where she shared fitness tips and healthy lifestyle content.

She was also a passionate supporter of Corinthians football club. Tributes are expected to pour in as friends, family and fans come to terms with the devastating loss.

It comes after two girls died after a horror crash involving their school bus in Tennessee. Zoe Davis and Arianna Pearson were among more than 20 pupils on the bus when it collided with a council refuse truck and a car on Friday. The Kenwood Middle School group were returning from a school trip when the accident happened in Carroll County, Tennessee.

Article continues below

The girls died of their injuries, leaving the families devastated. Patricia Shipley, a friend of Zoe's family, said: "We received the devastating news that our wonderful girl Zoe was one of the children killed in the bus accident in Carroll County. My friends are completely lost and heartbroken."
